```

Do not print, copy into the repository, or include the key values in a command
or test log. The file exports `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`; the
runner reads them from its environment. No run happens without Kenneth
approving that batch (case count, runs, token estimate). A `403 Key limit
exceeded` means stop; do not switch keys.

The model, hosts and judge are the printer suite's (`tests/printer_prompt`,
"Which model"): DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter, pinned to Alibaba,
Novita, Baidu and AtlasCloud, with a pinned OpenAI judge.

## One step, with its reads answered

Each case starts at a point recorded from the app and judges the model's next
step: a tool call or a reply. A read the case does not decide on (any
read-only tool, such as `workspace_inspect` before a reply) is answered with
the result the app gave for that read at the same point, and the model is
asked again, at most three times (`MAX_READS`). Nothing else is ever
answered: a change, or any call the case judges, is the outcome and ends the
run. A read with no recorded answer, or a fourth read, ends it unobserved. A
call with arguments the registry would refuse is never answered either; it is
the step, reported beside it, and refusals are the C++ tests' business.

The recorded answers, kept beside each request, are the reads the script's
`answers` list names:

- `workspace_inspect` and `slice_report` with every section, given whatever
  sections the model asked for, and `printer_list`;
- `object_analyze` for every object on every plate with every `include`
  but `measure`, given for that object and session whatever it included;
  never with `measure` or `candidates`;
- every setting, read with `settings_get`: of the print, of every object on
  every plate, of the selected filament and of the printer (355, 275 each,
  126 and 171 in the current recording). The keys come from the app itself:
  an empty `settings_search` query lists every setting of a scope, page by
  page. The filament's and printer's keys are also read under the print
  scope, and the print-wide settings under each object's scope, so a name
  asked for under the wrong scope gets the app's own answer, and so are three hand-kept lists of names the model takes from
  other slicers or invents (`fill_density`, `perimeters`,
  `initial_layer_height`...). A model's `settings_get` is answered with
  exactly the keys it asked for, in its order, each taken from those reads
  of the same scope and target, around the rest of the first such result;
- `settings_search` for 49 queries, given when the scope, target and
  words of the query match (case, spacing and word order aside), whatever
  `limit` or `writable` the model passed; never for `changedOnly`. A search
  result is the app's ranking for that query, so a wording not recorded has
  no answer.

They are real results the recorder got by calling those reads at that point
in the same turn; each case's point is replayed from the start for its own
recording, so those calls reach no other case's history. Recording all 23
points takes under three minutes. To keep `requests.json` small (about
3 MB), the recorder keeps each distinct setting item once, file-wide
(`settingItems`), and each point's workspace block once when a result
repeats it exactly (`sharedWorkspace`); the runner and the schema test put
both back byte for byte. A read outside these, or a `target` sent as a
string of JSON (which the app refuses), ends the run unobserved. Of the 38
distinct reads that ended runs unobserved in the runs of 2026-10-15, 26 are
now recorded; the other 12 are string targets, `changedOnly` searches,
search wordings not recorded, and setting names that do not exist in
OrcaSlicer.

This is not the design that failed on 2026-10-10. That one answered every
call, changes included, with stand-in results that did not hold what the
model asked for (`{"accepted": true}`), and let it run on: it wandered for 10
to 19 calls, provoked the behaviour it counted and spent over 300 million
tokens. Here only reads are answered, only with real results, and at most
three times. What this still gives up is whether the model chains changes on
its own across a conversation; only a run against the built app with real
results for every call can show that.

## What keeps it faithful to the app

  `tests/printer_prompt/render_prompt.mjs` (`"kind": "project"`) and the page's
  esbuild. This needs node and the AgentUI npm install. `--prompt-rev REV`
  renders it as it was at a git revision, 6b4b8b6188 or later (the commit
  that moved the prompt from C++ to the page, unchanged).
- **`project_tools.json`** is the tool list the app sends in the project chat

  ```

  chat's real OpenAI adapter, but the adapter's requests go nowhere: each is
  answered with the next model output the script gives. The tools run for
  real, and the app builds every request itself: the earlier turns as

  result over 16 KiB replaced by the omission note, at most 20 entries), the

  developer line, and the live results of this turn's calls with the

1. **Add knowledge or procedures the agent lacks.**  
   Assume the model already understands common concepts. Include application-specific behavior, non-obvious constraints, useful procedures, and known pitfalls. General advice such as “consider load direction” needs evidence of benefit to justify inclusion. Anthropic explicitly says: “Only add context Claude doesn’t already have.” [Authoring guidance](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices)

2. **Start from real work and demonstrated gaps.**  
   Complete representative tasks with the agent. Capture the corrections, missing context, and successful techniques that actually mattered. Existing code, support incidents, and expert procedures are stronger source material than asking an LLM to summarize a subject. The Agent Skills guidance specifically identifies skills generated solely from general training knowledge as a common failure mode. [Skill creation best practices](https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/best-practices)

3. **Organize each skill around a coherent capability.**  
   Its contents should belong together because they help accomplish a particular task. Splitting every tool operation into a skill creates overhead; grouping unrelated procedures into a broad topic makes selection less precise. The appropriate boundaries follow the useful procedure we discover. [Scope guidance](https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/best-practices)

4. **Make discovery precise and load detail progressively.**  
   The description explains when the skill helps. `SKILL.md` contains the essential procedure. Substantial conditional references, examples, or scripts are loaded only when needed. A short skill can be self-contained; additional folders are useful only when they contain something worth retrieving. 5. **Calibrate how prescriptive the instructions are.**  
   Use exact sequences for fragile operations with real ordering requirements. Leave judgment available for contextual decisions. Include concrete examples or executable helpers where they prevent recurring mistakes. Avoid accumulating universal rules from isolated failures. 6. **Measure the improvement the skill provides.**

2	JusPrin should interpret “print this” as a request to prepare the model, including resolving the printer, filament, and process configuration. Users should not have to request preset selection separately or know which skills to invoke. This preparation responsibility applies only when relevant to the user’s request; the agent must also answer questions and troubleshoot without unnecessarily changing the project.
3	
4	**Expected behavior**
5	
6	When asked to prepare or print a model, the agent should:
7	
8	1. Inspect the current project, printer setup, and existing preset selections.
9	2. Establish which filament will be used. Distinguish software configuration from physical facts: a selected filament preset does not prove that filament is loaded. Ask about consequential unknowns when available evidence cannot resolve them.
10	3. Select or retain suitable printer, filament, and process presets. A preset is a saved configuration; choosing a material and choosing its corresponding preset are related but distinct decisions.
11	4. Preserve suitable existing settings and customizations. Preparation does not require replacing every selection with a stock preset.
12	5. Slice and inspect the result against the user’s requirements. Revisit selections or settings when the evidence warrants it.
13	6. Proceed through the application’s Send preflight and authorization boundary. A request to prepare a print must not bypass that boundary.
14	
15	Material choice generally informs filament and process configuration, but these decisions can be revisited as constraints emerge.
16	
17	**Where the responsibilities belong**
18	
19	| Mechanism                             | Responsibility                                                                                              |
20	| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
21	| Core agent instructions               | Define the agent’s general role and the obligations that apply when preparing a print.                      |
22	| Live context and read tools           | Supply existing selections, available presets, printer capabilities, and known physical facts.              |
23	| Tool descriptions and execution tools | Explain and perform preset discovery, inspection, preview, and application.                                 |
24	| Optional skills                       | Supply specialized judgment or procedures when existing instructions and tools prove insufficient.          |
25	| Application code                      | Enforce objective validity, compatibility where detectable, freshness, and consequential-action boundaries. |
26	
27	The core instructions should describe a general responsibility, not special-case the literal phrase “get it printed.” Suggested wording:
28	
29	> You help users with 3D printing: answering questions, preparing prints, adjusting projects, and troubleshooting problems. Follow the user’s requested scope. Questions can be answered without changing the project.
30	>
31	> When the user asks you to prepare or print a model, establish a suitable printer, filament, and process configuration. Inspect existing choices before replacing them, resolve consequential unknowns, and verify the resulting slice before reporting readiness. Starting the physical print follows the app’s authorization boundary.
32	
33	**Skill design decisions**
34	
35	- No new “workflow” abstraction is required. That word referred only to the steps taken to fulfill a request.
36	- Explicit selection, such as “use the 0.20 mm Standard preset,” should normally use the existing tools directly.
37	- Preset-selection guidance can live inside a relevant skill when it adds useful judgment. Selecting presets does not itself justify a dedicated skill.
38	- A material-selection skill remains a candidate, not an agreed requirement. Its value must be demonstrated.
39	- Printer, filament, and process presets should not automatically be grouped into one skill merely because all are called presets.
40	
41	**Verification before calling the design reliable**
42	
43	Evaluate broad preparation requests with suitable existing settings, missing setup, incompatible imported presets, and unknown loaded filament. Verify that the agent preserves valid customizations, resolves actual gaps, and checks the resulting slice.
44	
45	Also test scope boundaries: “What is PETG?”, “Would PETG work here?”, and “Why did this warp?” must not automatically trigger project changes or a full preparation sequence.
46

187

189	   Its contents should belong together because they help accomplish a particular task. JusPrin should interpret “print this” as a request to prepare the model, including resolving the printer, filament, and process configuration. Users should not have to request preset selection separately or know which skills to invoke. This preparation responsibility applies only when relevant to the user’s request; the agent must also answer questions and troubleshoot without unnecessarily changing the project.

**Expected behavior**

When asked to prepare or print a model, the agent should:

1. Inspect the current project, printer setup, and existing preset selections.
2. Establish which filament will be used. Distinguish software configuration from physical facts: a selected filament preset does not prove that filament is loaded. Ask about consequential unknowns when available evidence cannot resolve them.
3. Select or retain suitable printer, filament, and process presets. A preset is a saved configuration; choosing a material and choosing its corresponding preset are related but distinct decisions.
4. Preserve suitable existing settings and customizations. Preparation does not require replacing every selection with a stock preset.
5. Slice and inspect the result against the user’s requirements. Revisit selections or settings when the evidence warrants it.
6. Proceed through the application’s Send preflight and authorization boundary. A request to prepare a print must not bypass that boundary.

Material choice generally informs filament and process configuration, but these decisions can be revisited as constraints emerge.

**Where the responsibilities belong**

| Mechanism                             | Responsibility                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Core agent instructions               | Define the agent’s general role and the obligations that apply when preparing a print.                      |
| Live context and read tools           | Supply existing selections, available presets, printer capabilities, and known physical facts.              |
| Tool descriptions and execution tools | Explain and perform preset discovery, inspection, preview, and application.                                 |
| Optional skills                       | Supply specialized judgment or procedures when existing instructions and tools prove insufficient.          |
| Application code                      | Enforce objective validity, compatibility where detectable, freshness, and consequential-action boundaries. |

The core instructions should describe a general responsibility, not special-case the literal phrase “get it printed.” Suggested wording:

> You help users with 3D printing: answering questions, preparing prints, adjusting projects, and troubleshooting problems. Follow the user’s requested scope. Questions can be answered without changing the project.
>
> When the user asks you to prepare or print a model, establish a suitable printer, filament, and process configuration. Inspect existing choices before replacing them, resolve consequential unknowns, and verify the resulting slice before reporting readiness. Starting the physical print follows the app’s authorization boundary.

**Skill design decisions**

- No new “workflow” abstraction is required. That word referred only to the steps taken to fulfill a request.
- Explicit selection, such as “use the 0.20 mm Standard preset,” should normally use the existing tools directly.
- Preset-selection guidance can live inside a relevant skill when it adds useful judgment. Selecting presets does not itself justify a dedicated skill.
- A material-selection skill remains a candidate, not an agreed requirement. Its value must be demonstrated.
- Printer, filament, and process presets should not automatically be grouped into one skill merely because all are called presets.

**Verification before calling the design reliable**

Evaluate broad preparation requests with suitable existing settings, missing setup, incompatible imported presets, and unknown loaded filament. Verify that the agent preserves valid customizations, resolves actual gaps, and checks the resulting slice.

Also test scope boundaries: “What is PETG?”, “Would PETG work here?”, and “Why did this warp?” must not automatically trigger project changes or a full preparation sequence.

These are agreed behavioral req

I couldn’t recover the exact earlier research transcript because this repository isn’t mirrored to Entire. I rechecked the primary sources. These are the best practices that should guide the design:

1. **Add knowledge or procedures the agent lacks.**  
   Assume the model already understands common concepts. Include application-specific behavior, non-obvious constraints, useful procedures, and known pitfalls. General advice such as “consider load direction” needs evidence of benefit to justify inclusion. Anthropic explicitly says: “Only add context Claude doesn’t already have.” [Authoring guidance](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices)

2. **Start from real work and demonstrated gaps.**  
   Complete representative tasks with the agent. Capture the corrections, missing context, and successful techniques that actually mattered. Existing code, support incidents, and expert procedures are stronger source material than asking an LLM to summarize a subject. The Agent Skills guidance specifically identifies skills generated solely from general training knowledge as a common failure mode. [Skill creation best practices](https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/best-practices)

3. **Organize each skill around a coherent capability.**  
   Its contents should belong together because they help accomplish a particular task. Splitting every tool operation into a skill creates overhead; grouping unrelated procedures into a broad topic makes selection less precise. The appropriate boundaries follow the useful procedure we discover. [Scope guidance](https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/best-practices)

4. **Make discovery precise and load detail progressively.**  
   The description explains when the skill helps. `SKILL.md` contains the essential procedure. Substantial conditional references, examples, or scripts are loaded only when needed. A short skill can be self-contained; additional folders are useful only when they contain something worth retrieving. [Skill architecture](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills)

5. **Calibrate how prescriptive the instructions are.**  
   Use exact sequences for fragile operations with real ordering requirements. Leave judgment available for contextual decisions. Include concrete examples or executable helpers where they prevent recurring mistakes. Avoid accumulating universal rules from isolated failures. [Authoring guidance](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices)

6. **Measure the improvement the skill provides.**  
   Establish what happens without it, add the minimum guidance needed, then compare meaningful outcomes. Discovery and loading are separate checks from usefulness. A few representative tasks can expose whether a skill adds value; this needn’t become a large benchmark. [Evaluation guidance](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices#evaluation-and-iteration)

- Advice about walls, infill, moisture, warping, and asking discriminating questions is largely generic.
- Guidance connecting JusPrin’s geometry handles, semantic regions, setting scopes, and slice-report sections is a more promising contribution—but it needs concrete, verified procedures.

######## ecd1926a72
ecd1926a72 2026-09-17 00:59:08 +0000
Let a slice wait for its result, and record the M5 eval

slice_start takes wait: the call stays running, without holding up other
calls, until the run it started ends, and then says whether the plates are
sliced, so an agent can read slice_report next instead of ending its turn
mid-slice.

From the in-app runs: the region kinds now say which put the seam on a
face and which keep it off; unknown setting names count "enable" when
another word matches, so support_enable suggests enable_support; a search
term inside a key ranks with keys that start with it; and a feature handle
of the wrong kind says what kind it is.

The guide records the M5 eval: the MCP run passes; five in-app runs, none
of which met the whole request, with what each found.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

######## 303c835914
303c835914 2026-09-16 21:11:23 +0000
Lay out plates, import and delete, and retire the three fixture tools

plate_layout sets copies, printable, plate, name and extruder per object,
adds, names and types plates, and arranges as Orca's own job (reported
under a handle in the slicing section with what did not fit), in one
undo step through Orca's instance commands, the object list's printable
steps, Selection moves and PartPlate calls.

object_import (in-app, from a chat attachment) and object_import_file
(MCP, from an approved path shown on the card) share
IWorkspace::import_objects: load_files with LoadModel, the load-path
questions answered by the same rule as project_open, and each new
object's size in the result. project_delete_items deletes objects,
parts, copies and plates in one undo step, refusing up front the cases
Orca would report with an error dialog after returning. object_analyze
mesh lists parts with ids, and faces carry their side lengths.

duplicate_object, import_model and inspect_selection are retired; the
tests, the deterministic mock agent and the live regression now use
plate_layout, object_import and workspace_inspect.

Found on the way and fixed: the Agent page's test hook sent the first
render's attachment list, so an attached file never reached the agent;
the project_open record kept through a project replacement shared its
action id with the new project's first actions (it is now dropped once
reported, the host ignores activities from a closed session, and the
adapter clears its job list on replacement); and every mutating
description now says that calling the tool shows the approval card,
after the live model once read "waits for approval" as a precondition.

M3 eval: pass over MCP (inches block imported, unitsFix, named face
down, two copies arranged inside the plate). In-app with OpenAI the
tool sequence is right but the pinned model put the wrong face down in
two of the last three runs; recorded in the guide as an eval failure.
Harness default, --mcp, --mcp-bridge and --live-agent pass; agent tests
191 cases; Agent page tests 131; Python bridge suite green. Catalog:
in-app 20 definitions / 19,331 bytes, MCP 21 / 22,661.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

######## d13a7658c9
d13a7658c9 2026-09-16 04:32:56 +0000
Start Orca's slicing run from a tool, and read it back

slice_start posts Orca's own toolbar events after selecting the plate, which
is exactly what the fork's header button does. That keeps one owner for
slicing: the slice-all bookkeeping, the Prepare switch, and the auto-preview
rule all travel with those events, and no OrcaSlicer-owned line changes.

The call returns when the run has started, not when it ends. Waiting would
mean a second job engine; instead the handle it returns names the run, and
workspace_inspect's new slicing section reports what the slicer is doing and
what each plate currently holds. Running is a property of the workspace rather
than of a plate, because one background process serves the whole application.

Two refusals worth stating. Nothing in Orca records who started a run, so a
slice already in flight may be the person's: a second start is refused unless
the caller passes preempt, and preempt brings back the approval card that
slicing is otherwise exempt from. That is the first argument-sensitive
approval decision, so it lives in the registry beside the other two.

Catalog after: MCP 8 definitions, in-app 10 definitions and 5,821 bytes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

######## 39c2f7a781
39c2f7a781 2026-09-16 05:29:50 +0000
List the presets this installation actually offers

presets_list pages the printer, filament, and process collections with the
name a selection takes, the label the user sees, the vendor bundle, and
whether each is a system preset, selected, and compatible.

It reports Orca's cached compatibility verdict and never asks for a fresh one.
Asking is not read-only: update_compatible rewrites the flag on every preset,
flips default-preset visibility, and can change the selection outright, and
even evaluating one preset's condition inserts a key into its config. The
fork's own filament listing already made that choice; this follows it rather
than deriving the rule a second time.

Three more things the sources make necessary. Hidden and default presets are
skipped: hidden means this installation does not offer it, and a default is
Orca's placeholder, not something anyone prints with. What a project prints
with is the bundle's per-extruder filament choice, not the filament tab's
selection, so that is what "selected" means for filaments. And the bundle is
held const throughout, because the non-const accessors can select a preset
when the current index is out of range.

The page reports the total it is a page of, so an agent knows to follow the
cursor rather than treating one page as the catalogue.

Also folds the settings module's case-folding helper into one ascii_lower
rather than adding a second one beside it.

Catalog after: MCP 10 definitions and 7,670 bytes, in-app 12 and 7,112.

######## 0f46943de2
0f46943de2 2026-10-13 08:12:34 -0700
Hand OrcaSlicer's edit-time questions to the agent as preview warnings

When a person changes certain settings in OrcaSlicer's settings panel,
OrcaSlicer asks a question first: "smooth timelapse needs a prime tower,
enable it?", "this will change the shape of your model, are you sure?",
"change the recommended support settings for you?". The code that asks is
Tab::on_value_change, which runs for one field at a time. The settings tools
apply a patch through Tab::load_config, which never runs it. Since the tools
were allowed to change every setting except a short blacklist (5dadfe2801),
a patch could change these settings and nobody was asked or told.

settings_preview_patch now returns one warning per question, with code
orca_question:

- key: the setting the question is about;
- message: the question as a person would read it, whole;
- suggestions: the values OrcaSlicer's Yes would set, as key=value,
  leaving out any that already hold;

Start Orca's slicing run from a tool, and read it back

slice_start posts Orca's own toolbar events after selecting the plate, which
is exactly what the fork's header button does. That keeps one owner for
slicing: the slice-all bookkeeping, the Prepare switch, and the auto-preview
rule all travel with those events, and no OrcaSlicer-owned line changes.

The call returns when the run has started, not when it ends. Waiting would
mean a second job engine; instead the handle it returns names the run, and
workspace_inspect's new slicing section reports what the slicer is doing and
what each plate currently holds. Running is a property of the workspace rather
than of a plate, because one background process serves the whole application.

Two refusals worth stating. Nothing in Orca records who started a run, so a
slice already in flight may be the person's: a second start is refused unless
the caller passes preempt, and preempt brings back the approval card that
slicing is otherwise exempt from. That is the first argument-sensitive
approval decision, so it lives in the registry beside the other two.

presets_list pages the printer, filament, and process collections with the

It reports Orca's cached compatibility verdict and never asks for a fresh one.
Asking is not read-only: update_compatible rewrites the flag on every preset,
flips default-preset visibility, and can change the selection outright, and
even evaluating one preset's condition inserts a key into its config. The
fork's own filament listing already made that choice; this follows it rather
than deriving the rule a second time.

skipped: hidden means this installation does not offer it, and a default is
Orca's placeholder, not something anyone prints with. What a project prints
with is the bundle's per-extruder filament choice, not the filament tab's
selection, so that is what "selected" means for filaments. And the bundle is
held const throughout, because the non-const accessors can select a preset
when the current index is out of range.

The page reports the total it is a page of, so an agent knows to follow the
cursor rather than treating one page as the catalogue.
